questions.question_text: Following are statements of a few processes taking place in nature. I. Free expansion of a gas II. The combustion of a mixture of petrol and air ignited by a spark III. The leaking of gas from the kitchen cylinder. IV. The transfer of heat from one heated part of a liquid to the other colder part. Which amongst these processes are irreversible in nature?
questions.question_html:
Following are statements of a few processes taking place in nature.
I. Free expansion of a gas
II. The combustion of a mixture of petrol and air ignited by a spark
III. The leaking of gas from the kitchen cylinder.
IV. The transfer of heat from one heated part of a liquid to the other colder part.
Which amongst these processes are irreversible in nature?

options.label: A
options.html: I and II

options.label: B
options.html: I and III

options.label: C
options.html: II, III and IV

options.label: D
options.html: I, II, III and IV

questions.explanation_text: All the given processes are irreversible in nature. Free expansion of a gas is irreversible because the gas spreads into the available space on its own. It cannot return to its original volume without some external work being done. Combustion of petrol and air is also irreversible. Once petrol burns, it forms new substances like carbon dioxide, water vapour, etc. These products cannot change back into petrol and air by simply reversing the process. Leaking of gas from a kitchen cylinder is irreversible because the gas moves from high pressure inside the cylinder to lower pressure outside. It will not collect back into the cylinder on its own. Transfer of heat from a hotter part of a liquid to a colder part is irreversible because heat naturally flows from higher temperature to lower temperature. The reverse does not happen by itself. So, all four processes are irreversible. $\text{Option D: I, II, III and IV}$
questions.explanation_html:
All the given processes are irreversible in nature.

Free expansion of a gas is irreversible because the gas spreads into the available space on its own. It cannot return to its original volume without some external work being done.

Combustion of petrol and air is also irreversible. Once petrol burns, it forms new substances like carbon dioxide, water vapour, etc. These products cannot change back into petrol and air by simply reversing the process.

Leaking of gas from a kitchen cylinder is irreversible because the gas moves from high pressure inside the cylinder to lower pressure outside. It will not collect back into the cylinder on its own.

Transfer of heat from a hotter part of a liquid to a colder part is irreversible because heat naturally flows from higher temperature to lower temperature. The reverse does not happen by itself.

So, all four processes are irreversible.

$\text{Option D: I, II, III and IV}$

questions.question_html: In thermodynamic processes, which of the following statements is not true?

options.label: A
options.text: In an isothermal process, the temperature remains constant
options.html: In an isothermal process, the temperature remains constant

options.label: B
options.text: In an isobaric process, the volume remains constant
options.html: In an isobaric process, the volume remains constant

options.label: C
options.text: In an adiabatic process, the system is insulated from the surroundings
options.html: In an adiabatic process, the system is insulated from the surroundings

options.label: D
options.text: In an adiabatic process, $PV^{\gamma}=$ a constant
options.html: In an adiabatic process, $PV^{\gamma}=$ a constant

questions.explanation_text: The statement that is not true is: $\text{Option B}$ In an isobaric process, the pressure remains constant, not the volume. The word “isobaric” means constant pressure. So for an isobaric process, $P=\text{constant}$ If the volume remains constant, that process is called an isochoric process. The other statements are correct: In an isothermal process, $T=\text{constant}$ In an adiabatic process, no heat is exchanged with the surroundings, so the system is insulated: $Q=0$ Also, for a reversible adiabatic process of an ideal gas, $PV^{\gamma}=\text{constant}$ So the incorrect statement is Option B.
questions.explanation_html:
The statement that is not true is:

$\text{Option B}$

In an isobaric process, the pressure remains constant, not the volume.

The word “isobaric” means constant pressure. So for an isobaric process,

$P=\text{constant}$

If the volume remains constant, that process is called an isochoric process.

The other statements are correct:

In an isothermal process,

$T=\text{constant}$

In an adiabatic process, no heat is exchanged with the surroundings, so the system is insulated:

$Q=0$

Also, for a reversible adiabatic process of an ideal gas,

$PV^{\gamma}=\text{constant}$

So the incorrect statement is Option B.

questions.question_text: A gas is taken from state A to state B along two different paths 1 and 2. The heat absorbed and work done by the system along these two paths are $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ and $W_{1}$ and $W_{2}$ respectively. Then
questions.question_html: A gas is taken from state A to state B along two different paths 1 and 2. The heat absorbed and work done by the system along these two paths are $Q_{1}$ and $Q_{2}$ and $W_{1}$ and $W_{2}$ respectively. Then
questions.explanation_text: According to the first law of thermodynamics, the change in internal energy ( $\Delta U$ ) of a system can be expressed as: $\Delta U=Q-W$ Where $Q$ is the heat absorbed by the system and $W$ is the work done by the system. For paths 1 and 2 from state A to state B, the change in internal energy is the same, regardless of the path taken: $\Delta U_{1}=\Delta U_{2}$ Therefore, the heat absorbed and work done along the different paths follows the relationship: $Q_{1}-W_{1}=Q_{2}-W_{2}$ This equation signifies that the net change in energy (considering both heat and work) is equal for both paths due to the same change in internal energy from state A to state B.
questions.explanation_html:
According to the first law of thermodynamics, the change in internal energy ( $\Delta U$ ) of a system can be expressed as:

$\Delta U=Q-W$

Where $Q$ is the heat absorbed by the system and $W$ is the work done by the system.

For paths 1 and 2 from state A to state B, the change in internal energy is the same, regardless of the path taken:

$\Delta U_{1}=\Delta U_{2}$

Therefore, the heat absorbed and work done along the different paths follows the relationship:

$Q_{1}-W_{1}=Q_{2}-W_{2}$

This equation signifies that the net change in energy (considering both heat and work) is equal for both paths due to the same change in internal energy from state A to state B.

questions.question_text: At $27^{\circ}C$ temperature, the mean kinetic energy of the atoms of an ideal gas is $E_{1}$ . If the temperature is increased to $327^{\circ}C$ , then the mean kinetic energy of the atoms will be
questions.question_html: At $27^{\circ}C$ temperature, the mean kinetic energy of the atoms of an ideal gas is $E_{1}$ . If the temperature is increased to $327^{\circ}C$ , then the mean kinetic energy of the atoms will be
questions.explanation_text: The mean kinetic energy of the atoms in an ideal gas is directly proportional to the temperature measured in Kelvin. At an initial temperature of 27°C, the mean kinetic energy is $E_{1}$ . When the temperature is increased to 327°C, we can determine the new mean kinetic energy $E_{2}$ using the relationship: $\frac{E_{1}}{E_{2}}=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}$ To find $E_{2}$ , we can rearrange this equation: $E_{2}=E_{1}\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}$ Converting the given temperatures from Celsius to Kelvin: Initial temperature, $T_{1}=27^{\circ}C+273=300K$ Final temperature, $T_{2}=327^{\circ}C+273=600K$ Substituting these values into the equation: $E_{2}=E_{1}(\frac{600}{300})=E_{1} \times 2=2E_{1}$ Therefore, when the temperature increases to 327°C, the mean kinetic energy of the atoms will be $2E_{1}$ .
questions.explanation_html:
The mean kinetic energy of the atoms in an ideal gas is directly proportional to the temperature measured in Kelvin. At an initial temperature of 27°C, the mean kinetic energy is $E_{1}$ . When the temperature is increased to 327°C, we can determine the new mean kinetic energy $E_{2}$ using the relationship:

$\frac{E_{1}}{E_{2}}=\frac{T_{1}}{T_{2}}$

To find $E_{2}$ , we can rearrange this equation:

$E_{2}=E_{1}\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}}$

Converting the given temperatures from Celsius to Kelvin:

Initial temperature, $T_{1}=27^{\circ}C+273=300K$

Final temperature, $T_{2}=327^{\circ}C+273=600K$

Substituting these values into the equation:

$E_{2}=E_{1}(\frac{600}{300})=E_{1} \times 2=2E_{1}$

Therefore, when the temperature increases to 327°C, the mean kinetic energy of the atoms will be $2E_{1}$ .

questions.question_text: Three metal rods of the same material and identical in all respects are joined as shown in the figure. The temperatures at the ends of these rods are maintained as indicated. Assuming no heat energy loss occurs through the curved surfaces of the rods, the temperature at the junction x is
questions.question_html: Three metal rods of the same material and identical in all respects are joined as shown in the figure. The temperatures at the ends of these rods are maintained as indicated. Assuming no heat energy loss occurs through the curved surfaces of the rods, the temperature at the junction x is
questions.explanation_text: To determine the temperature at the junction $x$ of three identical metal rods, follow this analysis: Assuming No Heat Loss : The rods are made of the same material and are identical, ensuring consistent heat flow throughout. Thermal Resistance : Let the thermal resistance of each rod be $R$ . The temperature at the junction is $T_{x}$ . Heat Flow Equilibrium : Since the system reaches a steady state, the heat flowing into the junction from each side should equal the heat flowing out: $H=H_{1}+H_{2}$ Where: $H$ is the heat flowing into the junction from both ends. $H_{1}$ and $H_{2}$ are the heat flows from the sides of the junction. Application : Set up the heat balance equation: $\frac{T_{x}-0}{R}=\frac{90-T_{x}}{R}+\frac{90-T_{x}}{R}$ Simplifying : Substitute and solve: $T_{x}=\frac{180}{3}=60^{\circ}\text{C}$ Therefore, the temperature at the junction $x$ is $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ . This calculation assumes perfect thermal conduction and no heat loss outside the system.
questions.explanation_html:
To determine the temperature at the junction $x$ of three identical metal rods, follow this analysis:

Assuming No Heat Loss: The rods are made of the same material and are identical, ensuring consistent heat flow throughout.

Thermal Resistance: Let the thermal resistance of each rod be $R$ . The temperature at the junction is $T_{x}$ .

Heat Flow Equilibrium: Since the system reaches a steady state, the heat flowing into the junction from each side should equal the heat flowing out:

$H=H_{1}+H_{2}$

Where:

$H$ is the heat flowing into the junction from both ends.

$H_{1}$ and $H_{2}$ are the heat flows from the sides of the junction.

Application: Set up the heat balance equation:

$\frac{T_{x}-0}{R}=\frac{90-T_{x}}{R}+\frac{90-T_{x}}{R}$

Simplifying: Substitute and solve:

$T_{x}=\frac{180}{3}=60^{\circ}\text{C}$

Therefore, the temperature at the junction $x$ is $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ . This calculation assumes perfect thermal conduction and no heat loss outside the system.

The ratio of the velocities $v$ and $v_{\text{rms}}$ for helium and oxygen gases are $X$ and $X^{'}$ respectively. Then, $\frac{X}{X^{'}}$ is equal to
questions.explanation_text: The speed of sound at a given temperature is given by $v_{\text{sound}}=\sqrt{\frac{rRT}{M}} \Rightarrow v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$ For oxygen molecules; $\frac{v_{O}}{v_{rms}}=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{r_{O}RT}{M}}}{\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}}=\sqrt{\frac{r_{O}}{3}}$ For helium molecules; $\frac{v_{He}}{v_{rms}}=\frac{\sqrt{r_{He}\frac{RT}{M}}}{\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}}=\sqrt{\frac{r_{He}}{3}}(r_{He}=\frac{5}{3},r_{O}=\frac{7}{5})$ $\frac{x^{'}}{x}=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{5}{9}}}{\sqrt{\frac{7}{15}}}=\sqrt{\frac{25}{21}}=\frac{5}{\sqrt{21}}$
questions.explanation_html:
The speed of sound at a given temperature is given by

$v_{\text{sound}}=\sqrt{\frac{rRT}{M}} \Rightarrow v_{\text{rms}}=\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}$

For oxygen molecules; $\frac{v_{O}}{v_{rms}}=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{r_{O}RT}{M}}}{\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}}=\sqrt{\frac{r_{O}}{3}}$

For helium molecules; $\frac{v_{He}}{v_{rms}}=\frac{\sqrt{r_{He}\frac{RT}{M}}}{\sqrt{\frac{3RT}{M}}}=\sqrt{\frac{r_{He}}{3}}(r_{He}=\frac{5}{3},r_{O}=\frac{7}{5})$

$\frac{x^{'}}{x}=\frac{\sqrt{\frac{5}{9}}}{\sqrt{\frac{7}{15}}}=\sqrt{\frac{25}{21}}=\frac{5}{\sqrt{21}}$

questions.question_html: A gas mixture contains monoatomic and diatomic molecules of 2 moles each. The mixture has a total internal energy of (symbols have usual meanings)
questions.explanation_text: Total internal energy of a gas is given as $U=\frac{n}{2}fRT$ where, $n=$ number of moles and $f=$ degree of freedom. Given, $n_{\text{diatomic}}=n_{\text{monoatomic}}=2$ As, $f_{\text{monoatomic}}=3$ $\begin{aligned} f_{\text{diatomic}} & =5 \\ \Rightarrow U_{\text{monoatomic}} & =\frac{2}{2} \times 3RT=3RT \\ U_{\text{diatomic}} & =\frac{2}{2} \times 5RT=5RT \end{aligned}$ $\therefore$ Total internal energy of the mixture of gases, $\begin{aligned} U_{\text{total}} & =U_{\text{monoatomic}}+U_{\text{diatomic}} \\ & =3RT+5RT=8RT \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:

$U=\frac{n}{2}fRT$

where, $n=$ number of moles

and $f=$ degree of freedom.

$\therefore$ Total internal energy of the mixture of gases,

$\begin{aligned} U_{\text{total}} & =U_{\text{monoatomic}}+U_{\text{diatomic}} \\ & =3RT+5RT=8RT \end{aligned}$

questions.explanation_text: Volume expansion is the expansion of volume of a gas due to increase in its temperature. $\therefore$ Coefficient of volume expansion is given as $\alpha_{V}=\frac{\Delta V}{V \times \Delta T}\text{.... (i)}$ where, $V=$ real volume of gas, $\Delta V=$ change in volume and $\Delta T=$ change in temperature. From ideal gas equation, $pV=nRT\text{or}T=\frac{pV}{nR}\text{.... (ii)}$ For constant pressure, $\begin{aligned} p\Delta V & =nR\Delta T \\ \text{or}\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta T} & =\frac{nR}{p}\text{.... (iii)} \end{aligned}$ From Eqs. (i) and (iii), we get $\alpha_{V}=\frac{nR}{pV}=\frac{1}{T}$ [ $\because$ From Eq. (ii)] Thus, the variation of $\alpha_{V}$ with temperature is correctly depicted in option (b).
questions.explanation_html:
Volume expansion is the expansion of volume of a gas due to increase in its temperature.

$\therefore$ Coefficient of volume expansion is given as

$\alpha_{V}=\frac{\Delta V}{V \times \Delta T}\text{.... (i)}$

where, $V=$ real volume of gas,

$\Delta V=$ change in volume

and $\Delta T=$ change in temperature.

From ideal gas equation,

$pV=nRT\text{or}T=\frac{pV}{nR}\text{.... (ii)}$

For constant pressure,

$\begin{aligned} p\Delta V & =nR\Delta T \\ \text{or}\frac{\Delta V}{\Delta T} & =\frac{nR}{p}\text{.... (iii)} \end{aligned}$

From Eqs. (i) and (iii), we get

$\alpha_{V}=\frac{nR}{pV}=\frac{1}{T}$ [ $\because$ From Eq. (ii)]

Thus, the variation of $\alpha_{V}$ with temperature is correctly depicted in option (b).

questions.question_text: A certain amount of heat energy is supplied to a monoatomic ideal gas which expands at constant pressure. What fraction of the heat energy is converted into work?
questions.question_html: A certain amount of heat energy is supplied to a monoatomic ideal gas which expands at constant pressure. What fraction of the heat energy is converted into work?
questions.explanation_text: Suppose Q amount of heat is supplied to monoatomic gas which expands at constant pressure. This heat is then converted into the internal energy and work. According to the first law of thermodynamics, $\begin{aligned} Q & =U+W \\ \text{or}nC_{p}\Delta T & =nC_{V}\Delta T+W \end{aligned}$ where, $C_{p}$ and $C_{V}$ are the specific heat capacity at constant pressure and volume, respectively. $\therefore$ The fraction of heat converted to work is given as $\frac{W}{Q}=\frac{nC_{p}\Delta T-nC_{V}\Delta T}{nC_{p}\Delta T}$ For monoatomic gas, $n=1$ $\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \frac{W}{Q}=\frac{C_{p}-C_{V}}{C_{p}} & =\frac{\frac{5}{2}R-\frac{3}{2}R}{\frac{5}{2}R} \\ & =\frac{R}{\frac{5}{2}R}=\frac{2}{5} \end{aligned}$
questions.explanation_html:

where, $C_{p}$ and $C_{V}$ are the specific heat capacity at constant pressure and volume, respectively.

$\therefore$ The fraction of heat converted to work is given as

$\frac{W}{Q}=\frac{nC_{p}\Delta T-nC_{V}\Delta T}{nC_{p}\Delta T}$

For monoatomic gas, $n=1$

$\begin{aligned} \Rightarrow \frac{W}{Q}=\frac{C_{p}-C_{V}}{C_{p}} & =\frac{\frac{5}{2}R-\frac{3}{2}R}{\frac{5}{2}R} \\ & =\frac{R}{\frac{5}{2}R}=\frac{2}{5} \end{aligned}$

As heated at constant. pressure, using

questions.explanation_text: The kinetic energy of molecules in an ideal gas depends solely on the temperature. When the temperature remains constant, the average kinetic energy also remains constant. To explain further: The average kinetic energy per molecule in an ideal gas is given by: $⟨KE⟩=\frac{3}{2}kT,$ where: $k$ is the Boltzmann constant. $T$ is the temperature in Kelvin. Even if the pressure increases (which, according to the ideal gas law $PV=nRT$ , could happen by compressing the gas or by adding more molecules), as long as the temperature $T$ is held constant, the average kinetic energy $⟨KE⟩$ remains the same. Thus, the answer is: Option C: remains same.

questions.question_text: A cup of tea cools from $65.5^{\circ}C$ to $62.5^{\circ}C$ in 1 min in a room at $22.5^{\circ}C$ . How long will it take to cool from $46.5^{\circ}C$ to $40.5^{\circ}C$ in the same room?
questions.question_html: A cup of tea cools from $65.5^{\circ}C$ to $62.5^{\circ}C$ in 1 min in a room at $22.5^{\circ}C$ . How long will it take to cool from $46.5^{\circ}C$ to $40.5^{\circ}C$ in the same room?
questions.explanation_text: According to Newton's law of cooling, the rate of cooling is proportional to the difference between the object's temperature and the ambient temperature. We can express this relationship with the following equation: $\frac{\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}}{t}=\alpha(\frac{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}}{2}-\theta_{0})$ Where: $\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ are the initial and final temperatures respectively $t$ is the time it takes to cool $\alpha$ is a constant related to the cooling conditions $\theta_{0}$ is the ambient temperature Given: For the initial cooling from 65.5°C to 62.5°C in 1 minute with an ambient temperature of 22.5°C , we utilize the formula: $\frac{65.5-62.5}{1}=\alpha(\frac{65.5+62.5}{2}-22.5)$ For cooling from 46.5°C to 40.5°C in time $t$ , under the same ambient conditions: $\frac{46.5-40.5}{t}=\alpha(\frac{46.5+40.5}{2}-22.5)$ By solving Equations (i) and (ii), we determine the time $t$ for the second stage of cooling. In the calculations shown, we find: $t=4\text{minutes}$
questions.explanation_html:
According to Newton's law of cooling, the rate of cooling is proportional to the difference between the object's temperature and the ambient temperature. We can express this relationship with the following equation:

$\frac{\theta_{1}-\theta_{2}}{t}=\alpha(\frac{\theta_{1}+\theta_{2}}{2}-\theta_{0})$

Where:

$\theta_{1}$ and $\theta_{2}$ are the initial and final temperatures respectively

$t$ is the time it takes to cool

$\alpha$ is a constant related to the cooling conditions

$\theta_{0}$ is the ambient temperature

Given:

For the initial cooling from 65.5°C to 62.5°C in 1 minute with an ambient temperature of 22.5°C, we utilize the formula:

$\frac{65.5-62.5}{1}=\alpha(\frac{65.5+62.5}{2}-22.5)$

For cooling from 46.5°C to 40.5°C in time $t$ , under the same ambient conditions:

$\frac{46.5-40.5}{t}=\alpha(\frac{46.5+40.5}{2}-22.5)$

By solving Equations (i) and (ii), we determine the time $t$ for the second stage of cooling. In the calculations shown, we find:

$t=4\text{minutes}$

questions.question_text: A Carnot engine takes 300 calories of heat from a source at 500 K and rejects 150 calories of heat to the sink. The temperature of the sink is
questions.question_html: A Carnot engine takes 300 calories of heat from a source at 500 K and rejects 150 calories of heat to the sink. The temperature of the sink is
questions.explanation_text: For a Carnot engine, the ratio of the heat rejected to the heat absorbed is equal to the ratio of the temperatures of the cold sink to the hot source. This relationship is given by: $\frac{Q_{C}}{Q_{H}}=\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}$ Given: Heat absorbed, $Q_{H}=300\text{calories}$ Heat rejected, $Q_{C}=150\text{calories}$ Temperature of the hot source, $T_{H}=500\text{K}$ We can substitute these values into the equation: $\frac{150}{300}=\frac{T_{C}}{500}$ Simplify the left side: $\frac{1}{2}=\frac{T_{C}}{500}$ Now, solve for $T_{C}$ by multiplying both sides by 500: $T_{C}=\frac{500}{2}=250\text{K}$ Therefore, the temperature of the sink is 250 K, which corresponds to: Option B.
questions.explanation_html:
For a Carnot engine, the ratio of the heat rejected to the heat absorbed is equal to the ratio of the temperatures of the cold sink to the hot source. This relationship is given by:

$\frac{Q_{C}}{Q_{H}}=\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}$

Given:

Heat absorbed, $Q_{H}=300\text{calories}$

Heat rejected, $Q_{C}=150\text{calories}$

Temperature of the hot source, $T_{H}=500\text{K}$

We can substitute these values into the equation:

$\frac{150}{300}=\frac{T_{C}}{500}$

Simplify the left side:

$\frac{1}{2}=\frac{T_{C}}{500}$

Now, solve for $T_{C}$ by multiplying both sides by 500:

$T_{C}=\frac{500}{2}=250\text{K}$

Therefore, the temperature of the sink is 250 K, which corresponds to:

Option B.

questions.explanation_text: The specific heat capacity is defined by the formula $c=\frac{Q}{m\Delta T}$ where: $Q$ is the heat energy (in Joules), $m$ is the mass (in kilograms), $\Delta T$ is the temperature change (in Kelvin). From the formula, you can see that the specific heat capacity has units of energy per unit mass per unit temperature change. This results in units of Joules per kilogram Kelvin, or $Jkg^{-1}K^{-1}.$ Thus, the SI unit of specific heat capacity is given by Option D.

questions.question_text: For which combination of working temperatures, the efficiency of Carnot's engine is the least?
questions.question_html: For which combination of working temperatures, the efficiency of Carnot's engine is the least?
questions.explanation_text: The efficiency of a Carnot engine is determined by the formula: $\eta=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}$ where: $T_{H}$ is the temperature of the hot reservoir. $T_{C}$ is the temperature of the cold reservoir. To find the combination with the least efficiency, we need to calculate $\eta$ for each option. Option A: $T_{H}=100K$ , $T_{C}=80K$ $\eta_{A}=1-\frac{80}{100}=1-0.8=0.2\text{or}20%$ Option B: $T_{H}=40K$ , $T_{C}=20K$ $\eta_{B}=1-\frac{20}{40}=1-0.5=0.5\text{or}50%$ Option C: $T_{H}=80K$ , $T_{C}=60K$ $\eta_{C}=1-\frac{60}{80}=1-0.75=0.25\text{or}25%$ Option D: $T_{H}=60K$ , $T_{C}=40K$ $\eta_{D}=1-\frac{40}{60} \approx 1-0.667 \approx 0.333\text{or}33.3%$ Comparing the efficiencies, the lowest efficiency is 20% in Option A. Thus, the combination with the least efficiency is: Option A: $100K,80K$ .
questions.explanation_html:
The efficiency of a Carnot engine is determined by the formula:

$\eta=1-\frac{T_{C}}{T_{H}}$

where:

$T_{H}$ is the temperature of the hot reservoir.

$T_{C}$ is the temperature of the cold reservoir.

To find the combination with the least efficiency, we need to calculate $\eta$ for each option.

Option A: $T_{H}=100K$ , $T_{C}=80K$

$\eta_{A}=1-\frac{80}{100}=1-0.8=0.2\text{or}20%$

Option B: $T_{H}=40K$ , $T_{C}=20K$

$\eta_{B}=1-\frac{20}{40}=1-0.5=0.5\text{or}50%$

Option C: $T_{H}=80K$ , $T_{C}=60K$

$\eta_{C}=1-\frac{60}{80}=1-0.75=0.25\text{or}25%$

Option D: $T_{H}=60K$ , $T_{C}=40K$

$\eta_{D}=1-\frac{40}{60} \approx 1-0.667 \approx 0.333\text{or}33.3%$

Comparing the efficiencies, the lowest efficiency is 20% in Option A.

Thus, the combination with the least efficiency is:

Option A: $100K,80K$ .

questions.question_html: The mean energy of a molecule of an ideal gas is
questions.explanation_text: For an ideal gas, each translational degree of freedom contributes an average energy of $\frac{1}{2}kT,$ where $k$ is the Boltzmann constant. A molecule in three-dimensional space has three translational degrees of freedom. Therefore, the total mean energy per molecule is: Energy per degree of freedom: $\frac{1}{2}kT$ Total energy for three degrees: $3 \times \frac{1}{2}kT=\frac{3}{2}kT$ Thus, the mean energy of a molecule of an ideal gas is $\frac{3}{2}kT$ , which corresponds to Option D.
questions.explanation_html:
For an ideal gas, each translational degree of freedom contributes an average energy of $\frac{1}{2}kT,$ where $k$ is the Boltzmann constant. A molecule in three-dimensional space has three translational degrees of freedom. Therefore, the total mean energy per molecule is:

Energy per degree of freedom: $\frac{1}{2}kT$

Total energy for three degrees: $3 \times \frac{1}{2}kT=\frac{3}{2}kT$

Thus, the mean energy of a molecule of an ideal gas is $\frac{3}{2}kT$ , which corresponds to Option D.
